title: GERD: Treat the Syndrome, Investigate Alarm Features
bottomLine: Typical reflux without alarm features is usually a clinical diagnosis and can be treated empirically. Dysphagia, GI bleeding, anemia, weight loss, persistent vomiting or new concerning symptoms require investigation rather than indefinite acid suppression.
recognize: Heartburn and regurgitation are typical; cough/hoarseness are less specific.
differentiate: ACS can mimic reflux; dysphagia may represent stricture, eosinophilic disease or malignancy.
assessment: Assess symptom pattern, nocturnal symptoms, dysphagia, bleeding, weight loss, medication triggers, pregnancy and cardiac risk.
workup: Endoscopy is reserved for alarm features, refractory symptoms or specific risk; routine imaging is not required for uncomplicated GERD.
management: Use lifestyle measures that fit the patient's triggers and an appropriate PPI trial; step down to the lowest effective regimen when long-term therapy is not required.
medicationSafety: Long-term PPI therapy should have a continuing indication; do not stop abruptly in severe erosive disease without a plan.
counselling: Avoid universal food-ban lists; target the patient's actual triggers and meal timing.
followUp: Reassess response and indication rather than renewing PPI indefinitely without review.
examTrap: Ordering endoscopy for every young patient with classic uncomplicated heartburn or, conversely, continuing PPI alone despite progressive dysphagia.
oneLinePearl: Typical GERD can be treated clinically; alarm features change the pathway.

title: Dyspepsia and H. pylori: Test, Treat, Confirm Eradication
bottomLine: Uncomplicated dyspepsia often uses a test-and-treat H. pylori strategy in appropriate patients. If H. pylori is treated, confirm eradication with a test of active infection after therapy rather than assuming symptom improvement means cure.
recognize: Epigastric pain/burning, early satiety or postprandial fullness define dyspepsia.
differentiate: Alarm features, significant NSAID use and older/high-risk presentations may require endoscopy; biliary, pancreatic and cardiac disease can mimic dyspepsia.
assessment: Assess bleeding, anemia, weight loss, vomiting, dysphagia, NSAIDs, family gastric cancer risk and prior H. pylori treatment.
workup: Use urea breath test or stool antigen for active infection when appropriate; serology does not confirm eradication.
management: Use a contemporary effective eradication regimen informed by local resistance and prior antibiotic exposure, then confirm cure.
medicationSafety: PPIs, antibiotics and bismuth affect test accuracy and must be held for the recommended interval before eradication testing.
counselling: Explain adherence to the full multidrug regimen and why repeat testing matters.
followUp: Document eradication; persistent symptoms after cure need a renewed differential.
examTrap: Using H. pylori antibody testing to prove treatment success.
oneLinePearl: H. pylori treatment is not complete until eradication is confirmed.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology guideline library
current H. pylori evidence and local Canadian resistance pathways

title: Upper GI Bleeding: Resuscitate Before Endoscopy
bottomLine: Hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis or melena with instability is a resuscitation problem before it is an endoscopy problem. Secure perfusion, assess anticoagulants and arrange urgent endoscopic management based on risk.
recognize: Peptic ulcer, varices and mucosal lesions are major causes; brisk upper bleeding can cause hematochezia.
differentiate: Hemoptysis is respiratory; iron/bismuth can darken stool without bleeding.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, orthostasis when safe, bleeding quantity, cirrhosis, NSAIDs, antithrombotics and comorbidities.
workup: CBC, chemistry, coagulation, type and screen/crossmatch and serial clinical reassessment are core; risk scores can support disposition but do not replace judgment.
management: Establish IV access and resuscitate; use IV PPI for suspected significant nonvariceal bleeding and vasoactive/antibiotic therapy when variceal hemorrhage is suspected under acute-care protocol.
medicationSafety: Reverse anticoagulation for life-threatening bleeding according to agent and thrombotic context; do not transfuse solely to normalize hemoglobin without considering stability and thresholds.
counselling: After stabilization, address NSAIDs, H. pylori and alcohol/portal-hypertension risks.
followUp: Ensure endoscopic findings and secondary prevention are carried forward after discharge.
examTrap: Sending a hypotensive patient directly for endoscopy without initial resuscitation.
oneLinePearl: GI bleeding kills by loss of circulating volume first—resuscitate while you localize.
sourceBasis: Canadian gastroenterology acute bleeding practice resources

title: Lower GI Bleeding: Severity Before Source
bottomLine: Hematochezia ranges from benign anorectal bleeding to major diverticular, ischemic or upper-GI hemorrhage. Assess stability, anemia and anticoagulation before assuming hemorrhoids.
recognize: Bright red blood on tissue with anal pain can fit fissure; painless large-volume bleeding may be diverticular; cramping pain with bloody diarrhea can be colitis.
differentiate: Brisk upper GI bleeding can present as hematochezia when transit is rapid.
assessment: Assess vital signs, quantity/frequency, abdominal pain, bowel change, weight loss, anticoagulants and colorectal cancer history.
workup: CBC and targeted endoscopic/imaging evaluation depend on severity and suspected source; persistent unexplained bleeding needs colorectal evaluation.
management: Resuscitate significant bleeding and correct the cause; do not attribute bleeding to hemorrhoids without age/risk-appropriate assessment.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs and antithrombotics affect both bleeding severity and management decisions.
counselling: Teach return precautions for recurrent heavy bleeding, syncope or worsening pain.
followUp: Close the loop on colonoscopy/imaging and pathology.
examTrap: Diagnosing hemorrhoids from rectal bleeding in an older patient with weight loss and iron deficiency.
oneLinePearl: Hemorrhoids are common; they are not a licence to stop the bleeding differential.

title: Appendicitis: Time-Dependent Abdominal Inflammation
bottomLine: Progressive periumbilical-to-RLQ pain, anorexia, nausea and focal tenderness supports appendicitis, but presentations vary at the extremes of age and in pregnancy. Suspected perforation or peritonitis needs urgent surgical care.
recognize: Pain often precedes vomiting; fever and leukocytosis support but do not prove the diagnosis.
differentiate: Ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, PID, gastroenteritis, Crohn disease and renal colic can mimic it.
assessment: Assess pregnancy possibility, migration/tempo of pain, peritoneal signs, hydration and sepsis.
workup: Use ultrasound preferentially in children/pregnancy when feasible; CT is highly accurate in many adults and chosen based on risk/context.
management: Keep suspected significant appendicitis NPO, provide analgesia/fluids and arrange surgical assessment; antibiotics are used per operative/nonoperative pathway.
medicationSafety: Analgesia does not need to be withheld to preserve the abdominal exam.
counselling: Explain why evolving symptoms may require reassessment even after an initially nondiagnostic visit.
followUp: Give explicit return precautions if imaging/observation does not confirm appendicitis.
examTrap: Withholding pain medication because it might 'mask' appendicitis.
oneLinePearl: Treat pain while you diagnose the abdomen.

title: Diverticulitis: Uncomplicated or Complicated?
bottomLine: Localized LLQ pain and systemic inflammation can suggest diverticulitis, but abscess, perforation, obstruction, fistula or sepsis changes management. Antibiotics are not automatically required for every mild uncomplicated case in an immunocompetent patient.
recognize: Fever, LLQ tenderness and bowel change are common.
differentiate: Colorectal cancer, IBD, ischemic colitis and gynecologic disease can mimic it.
assessment: Assess peritoneal signs, immune status, vomiting/obstruction, prior episodes and ability to hydrate/follow up.
workup: CT is used when diagnosis is uncertain, severe or complicated disease is possible; avoid routine CT for every mild recurrent classic episode if a safe pathway exists.
management: Use selective outpatient supportive care versus antibiotics/admission based on severity and complication risk; drain/surgical consult for abscess or perforation as indicated.
medicationSafety: Avoid reflexive broad-spectrum antibiotic use in low-risk uncomplicated cases; NSAIDs may worsen GI risk.
counselling: After recovery, individualized colon evaluation may be needed depending on prior colonoscopy and episode features.
followUp: Reassess persistent symptoms and exclude alternate diagnoses.
examTrap: Assuming all diverticulitis requires antibiotics and all nuts/seeds must be avoided forever.
oneLinePearl: The key diverticulitis question is complication risk, not whether the CT shows diverticula.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology practice resources

title: Acute Pancreatitis: Supportive Care and Cause Finding
bottomLine: Typical epigastric pain plus significant lipase elevation or characteristic imaging establishes pancreatitis; routine CT is not needed when the diagnosis is clear. Early fluids, analgesia and enteral nutrition are central while identifying gallstone, alcohol, triglyceride and medication causes.
recognize: Pain often radiates to the back and is associated with nausea/vomiting.
differentiate: Perforated ulcer, ACS, aortic disease and biliary disease can mimic pancreatitis.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, organ dysfunction, gallstone/alcohol history, triglycerides, medications and pregnancy.
workup: Use lipase, LFTs, electrolytes/renal function and RUQ ultrasound for biliary cause; reserve CT for diagnostic uncertainty or complication assessment.
management: Provide balanced fluid resuscitation guided by response, analgesia, antiemetics and early oral/enteral nutrition when tolerated; urgent ERCP is for cholangitis or selected persistent obstruction.
medicationSafety: Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated for sterile pancreatitis.
counselling: Address alcohol, gallstones and triglyceride prevention after recovery.
followUp: Arrange definitive gallstone management when indicated to prevent recurrence.
examTrap: Ordering immediate CT for every classic pancreatitis presentation or keeping all patients NPO for days without indication.
oneLinePearl: Pancreatitis is usually a clinical-laboratory diagnosis; CT is for uncertainty or complications.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology acute pancreatitis guidance

title: Biliary Pain: Colic, Cholecystitis, or Cholangitis?
bottomLine: Transient postprandial RUQ pain without systemic inflammation fits biliary colic; persistent RUQ pain/fever suggests cholecystitis; fever plus jaundice and biliary pain suggests ascending cholangitis and requires urgent antibiotics plus biliary drainage.
recognize: Cholangitis can progress to sepsis rapidly and may be atypical in older adults.
differentiate: Pancreatitis can coexist with gallstones; hepatitis and peptic disease can mimic RUQ pain.
assessment: Assess fever, jaundice, hypotension, confusion, vomiting and pregnancy.
workup: Use RUQ ultrasound and liver tests; MRCP/ERCP is selected when common-duct obstruction is suspected.
management: Analgesia and surgical follow-up for symptomatic stones; cholecystitis generally requires early surgical pathway; cholangitis needs urgent antimicrobials and source control.
medicationSafety: Do not treat cholangitis with antibiotics alone when obstruction persists.
counselling: Explain recurrence risk and definitive gallbladder management.
followUp: Ensure surgical or biliary follow-up is completed.
examTrap: Calling fever, jaundice and RUQ pain simple biliary colic.
oneLinePearl: Biliary pain plus infection plus obstruction is a drainage problem.

title: Acute Diarrhea: Hydration, Exposure, and C. difficile Risk
bottomLine: Most acute diarrhea is self-limited and needs hydration, not antibiotics. Bloody diarrhea, severe dehydration, fever, immunocompromise, outbreak/travel exposure or recent antibiotics/hospitalization changes testing and treatment.
recognize: C. difficile risk rises after antibiotic and health-care exposure; severe disease can cause ileus and toxic megacolon.
differentiate: Inflammatory diarrhea has blood/fever/severe pain; osmotic/viral illness is often watery and self-limited.
assessment: Assess volume status, stool frequency/blood, fever, travel, sick contacts, food/water exposure, antibiotics, hospitalization and immune status.
workup: Stool testing is targeted to severe/persistent/bloody/outbreak or C. difficile-risk cases; do not test formed stool for C. difficile.
management: Use oral rehydration when possible; treat specific bacterial/parasitic disease and C. difficile according to current guidance rather than empiric antibiotics for everyone.
medicationSafety: Avoid antimotility agents in severe inflammatory diarrhea or toxic megacolon concern.
counselling: Hand hygiene and infection-control advice depends on pathogen; alcohol hand rub is less effective against C. difficile spores than soap/water for contaminated hands.
followUp: Persistent diarrhea requires a broader infectious, inflammatory and malabsorption differential.
examTrap: Ordering C. difficile PCR on a formed stool from an asymptomatic patient after antibiotics.
oneLinePearl: Test the diarrheal syndrome, not the colonization risk alone.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada enteric infection resources

title: Constipation: Alarm Features Before Laxative Escalation
bottomLine: Constipation is commonly functional or medication-related, but obstruction, bleeding, anemia, weight loss, new late-onset symptoms or neurologic dysfunction require evaluation before chronic laxative escalation.
recognize: Opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium, dehydration and immobility are common contributors.
differentiate: Overflow diarrhea can occur with fecal impaction; bowel obstruction causes pain/distension/vomiting and absent passage of gas/stool.
assessment: Assess baseline bowel pattern, diet/fluids, medications, pelvic floor symptoms, neurologic disease and alarm features.
workup: Routine imaging/labs are unnecessary in uncomplicated chronic constipation; targeted thyroid/calcium/colorectal evaluation follows clinical clues.
management: Use fibre/fluid/activity when appropriate and osmotic/stimulant agents based on phenotype; opioid-induced constipation often needs proactive bowel regimen.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic magnesium laxatives in significant renal impairment; bulk agents can worsen obstruction/impaction if used incorrectly.
counselling: Normalize regular toileting and discuss pelvic-floor therapy when evacuation dysfunction is suspected.
followUp: Reassess treatment response and reconsider diagnosis if refractory.
examTrap: Adding fibre to a patient with suspected fecal impaction and bowel obstruction symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Before adding stool bulk, make sure stool can get out.

title: Irritable Bowel Syndrome: Positive Diagnosis With Red-Flag Guardrails
bottomLine: IBS can be diagnosed positively from a compatible chronic abdominal pain/bowel pattern when alarm features are absent. Repeated invasive testing is not required simply because symptoms are real and persistent.
recognize: Abdominal pain related to defecation with change in stool frequency/form is characteristic.
differentiate: IBD, celiac disease, colorectal cancer, endometriosis and microscopic colitis can mimic IBS in the right context.
assessment: Assess bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, anemia, family history, inflammatory features and diet/stress relationship.
workup: Use limited targeted testing such as celiac screening and inflammatory markers in selected diarrhea-predominant patients rather than extensive exclusion testing.
management: Use subtype-specific diet, fibre, antispasmodic, bowel-directed and gut-brain treatments with shared decision-making.
medicationSafety: Avoid opioids for chronic IBS pain; restrictive diets should be time-limited and dietitian-supported when possible.
counselling: Explain the disorder of gut-brain interaction without implying symptoms are imagined.
followUp: Reassess new alarm features or meaningful phenotype change.
examTrap: Ordering colonoscopy repeatedly for stable classic IBS in a young patient with no alarm features.
oneLinePearl: IBS is a positive diagnosis, not a diagnosis of endless exclusion.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology IBS guidance

title: Celiac Disease: Test Before the Gluten-Free Diet
bottomLine: Test for celiac disease while the patient is still consuming gluten. Starting a gluten-free diet before serology/biopsy can make diagnosis harder and creates lifelong dietary burden without confirmation.
recognize: Diarrhea, bloating, iron deficiency, osteoporosis, poor growth and dermatitis herpetiformis are possible presentations.
differentiate: Non-celiac gluten sensitivity and IBS do not have the same autoimmune serology/intestinal injury.
assessment: Assess family history, autoimmune disease, iron deficiency, growth/weight, bone disease and current gluten intake.
workup: Use tissue transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA as standard initial testing in many patients; IgG-based testing is needed with IgA deficiency. Endoscopic biopsy remains important in many diagnostic pathways.
management: Use a strict gluten-free diet after diagnosis with dietitian support and correction of nutritional deficiencies.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe unnecessary supplements indefinitely without rechecking deficiencies.
counselling: Teach hidden gluten/cross-contamination and the difference between medical necessity and fad restriction.
followUp: Track symptoms, serology and nutritional status.
examTrap: Telling a patient to stop gluten for a month before celiac testing.
oneLinePearl: Celiac testing works best before gluten disappears from the diet.

title: Hemorrhoids and Anal Fissure: Do Not Miss the Other Source
bottomLine: Painful tearing with defecation suggests fissure; painless bright bleeding/prolapse suggests internal hemorrhoids. Neither diagnosis should be used to explain away persistent bleeding, anemia or cancer-risk features.
recognize: Fissures are commonly posterior midline and associated with constipation; thrombosed external hemorrhoids can be acutely painful.
differentiate: Abscess causes severe pain/swelling/systemic symptoms; IBD, STI lesions and colorectal cancer can mimic anorectal symptoms.
assessment: Ask bowel habit, bleeding pattern, pain, pregnancy/postpartum, receptive anal sex/STI risk and systemic symptoms; inspect the area respectfully with consent.
workup: Further colorectal evaluation is based on age, anemia, persistent bleeding and screening status.
management: Use stool-softening strategies, topical/local therapy and procedural referral for refractory disease.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged topical steroid use without reassessment.
counselling: Address constipation and avoid shame around anorectal examination.
followUp: Confirm healing; persistent fissure/bleeding requires alternative diagnosis evaluation.
examTrap: Assuming bright red blood is hemorrhoidal in a patient with iron deficiency and no prior colorectal evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Common anorectal disease can coexist with important proximal disease.

title: Acute Abdomen and Bowel Obstruction: Surgical Until Safe
bottomLine: Peritonitis, severe distension with vomiting/obstipation, pain out of proportion, shock or free-air concern requires urgent surgical evaluation. Do not turn a surgical abdomen into an outpatient lab exercise.
recognize: Bowel obstruction causes colicky pain, vomiting, distension and obstipation; strangulation/ischemia may cause constant severe pain, fever or lactate rise.
differentiate: Ileus has diffuse dysmotility without a mechanical transition point; mesenteric ischemia can cause severe pain with initially modest exam findings.
assessment: Assess prior surgery/hernias, cancer, bowel sounds, peritoneal signs, hydration, perfusion and hernia orifices.
workup: Use CBC/chemistry/lactate and urgent abdominal imaging based on stability; pregnancy alters imaging choice but not the need to diagnose dangerous disease.
management: NPO, IV access, fluid/electrolyte correction, decompression when indicated and urgent surgical consultation for mechanical obstruction/ischemia/perforation.
medicationSafety: Avoid laxatives or prokinetics in suspected mechanical obstruction.
counselling: Explain that prior abdominal surgery can cause adhesive obstruction years later.
followUp: After resolution, address cause and recurrence prevention.
examTrap: Giving an enema to a distended vomiting patient with obstipation and suspected obstruction.
oneLinePearl: Obstipation plus vomiting plus distension is obstruction until proven otherwise.
sourceBasis: Canadian emergency and surgical practice principles
